concept.title: Relationships between tasks
concept.shortdesc: A relationship says how one task drives another. Each has one of the four types project plans use:

strow.stentry: The task starts after the other finishes
From the other's end to the task's start
The task starts no earlier than the other starts
The task finishes no earlier than the other finishes
The task finishes no earlier than the other starts
From the other's start to the task's end

conbody.p: A relationship belongs to both of its tasks, and each one's panel lists it under Relationships, named from that task's side: by this task's end, then the other task's end. Open Write the requirements and its relationship to Design reads Finish to start: that starts after this finishes; open Design and the same relationship reads Start to finish: this starts after that finishes. You can add, change or remove it from either one:

strow.stentry: Finish to start: that starts after this finishes
Start to start: that starts after this starts
Finish to finish: that finishes after this finishes
Start to finish: that finishes after this starts
Start to finish: this starts after that finishes
Start to start: this starts after that starts
Finish to finish: this finishes after that finishes
Finish to start: this finishes after that starts

conbody.p: To add one, choose how this task relates to the other, then the other task. A task can have several relationships, so two tasks can together decide when a third starts: Build the prototype can wait for Wheel guard design and for Electronics to finish. Two tasks have one relationship between them: setting another replaces it. Change a relationship in its row, or remove it with the cross.

section.title: Offsets
section.p: A relationship can carry an offset: time the driven task keeps after what the type asks for. Its unit is working days, elapsed days (calendar days, for a wait that does not stop at weekends) or a percentage of the driving task's duration (50% of a ten-day task is five working days). Start to start with an offset of 5 means the second task starts five working days after the first one starts; finish to start with an offset of 2 leaves two working days between the first task's end and the second's start. A negative offset lets the driven task begin that many days earlier.

Set it in the Offset field under the relationship, on either task, and press Enter or leave the field; a new relationship takes one in the add form. A relationship whose task does not keep its offset is Broken, and float and the critical path count the offset as time the task cannot use.

section.title: Recalculating the plan
section.p: In a manual plan, OpenV never moves a task on its own. Recalculate, above the chart, moves them when you ask: every task that another task drives, or that a constraint holds to a date, goes to the dates those ask for. Tick Only move tasks later to treat relationships as minimums: a task that already starts on or after the day asked is left where it is, and nothing is pulled earlier.

strow.stentry: Starts the working day after the other ends, plus the offset
Starts the day the other starts, plus the offset
Ends the day the other ends, plus the offset
Ends the day the other starts, plus the offset

section.p: Each task keeps its duration. A task driven by several others takes the latest date any of them asks for. A task that nothing drives stays where it is, and so does a task that is done. A driven task with sub-tasks moves them, by as many working days as it has to move. The page asks before it recalculates, and then says how many tasks moved; recalculating a plan that already agrees with its relationships moves nothing.

section.title: Drawing a relationship on the chart
section.p: Point at a bar, or select its task, and a small + appears at each end. Press one and drag to another bar: a line follows the pointer, and a label says what releasing would make. Which ends you join decides the type:

strow.stentry: Finish to start: the other task starts after this one finishes
Start to finish: the other task finishes after this one starts

section.p: Release over the left half of a bar for its start, the right half for its end. Release anywhere else, or press Escape, to abandon the line.

OpenV does not move a task when its dates break a relationship. It marks the relationship Broken, draws its arrow dashed and red, and leaves the dates to you. A relationship to a task that is done is never broken. A relationship that would make a loop, where two tasks end up waiting on each other, is refused.
